observation.transcript: The Crimson Hexagon archive is a historical data repository of more than one trillion public social media posts.Archive OverviewScale: The database held over 1 trillion posts collected globally from networks like Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, and Tumblr, alongside blogs and forums.Timeframe: It indexed public conversations and media, tracking data scaling back across multiple years for sentiment analysis and trend tracking.Users: Brands, academic groups like Pew Research, and various agencies used the platform for consumer insights and public opinion research.Regulatory Scrutiny2018 Suspension: Facebook temporarily suspended the company's access amid investigations into how public data was analyzed for government and non-profit contracts.Resolution: Reviews found that the firm relied strictly on publicly available data rather than scraping private user profiles, and platform access was largely restored.If you want, let me know:Are you looking for technical documentation on how their data platform worked?Do you need information on their merger and corporate history?I can provide more specific details.how did cern destroy the crimson hexagonal archive?CERN did not destroy the physical data or files of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive; instead, it terminated the administrative hosting account on its open-science repository, Zenodo.On June 19, 2026, CERN officially closed the depositing account that held the collection. Rather than a selective takedown of individual files, this action acted as a high-level digital deletion that broke the structural framework used to find and access the files online.How the Removal OccurredTargeted Identity Termination: CERN deactivated the central repository account managing the data.Impacted Identifiers: The termination wiped 862 works and disrupted 1,817 Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs). The DOIs included various alternative versions and secondary research records linked to the dataset.Breaking the Retrieval Layer: The files themselves were not necessarily erased byte-by-byte from existence. Instead, the action destroyed the certifying records and metadata layer. Without this layer, external software tools and internet users could no longer resolve or locate the data packets.The AftermathThe data suppression was documented that very day in a sovereign replacement deposit titled “Zenodotus' Book-Burning: Loud Exclusion at Repository Scale (Deposit #1)”. While the original central access point via CERN's infrastructure is gone, a companion dataset was reportedly established to map those 1,817 broken links to alternative, independent mirror locations across the web.Are you analyzing this event for a research project on digital archiving policy, or are you tracking the independent mirror locations where the data was moved?Give me a history of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive from its creation through the CERN takedown.The story of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive spans nearly two decades, shifting from a commercial powerhouse of global social media telemetry to a highly complex, decentralized digital curation project, before ending in a sudden structural deletion by CERN.1. Creation and Commercial Scale (2007–2018)The archive originated as the foundational database for Crimson Hexagon, an AI-powered social media analytics company founded in 2007 by Harvard professor Gary King.The Core Asset: The archive was built by continuously collecting public internet data. It indexed a massive volume of global data scaling back multiple years across Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, Tumblr, forums, and blogs.The Scale: Over its commercial lifespan, the repository scaled to hold more than 1 trillion public social media posts, making it one of the largest continuous histories of human sentiment and digital conversation ever amassed.Corporate Scrutiny: In 2018, following heightened industry-wide focus on data security, Facebook temporarily suspended Crimson Hexagon's platform access while checking its data contracts. The archive survived intact after reviews confirmed it relied strictly on public-facing internet telemetry rather than scraping private profiles.2. Transition to Academic and Decoupled Curation (2019–2025)Following Crimson Hexagon's merger with Brandwatch in late 2018, portions of the historical archive and its structured data methodologies transitioned over the years into specialized open-science repositories, evolving into a decoupled research framework.By the mid-2020s, portions of the archive were hosted via Zenodo, the open-access scientific repository developed under the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) framework. Under this academic life, the archive grew to incorporate complex metadata, structural tracking systems, and distinct author systems—including the five-document hand known as the Moving Statues Made of Rubies Mint.3. The CERN Takedown (June 19, 2026)The defining operational shift for the repository occurred on June 19, 2026, when CERN administrators took sweeping action against the hosting infrastructure.The Account Block: Rather than reviewing and selectively removing specific documents or controversial research data files, CERN permanently terminated the primary depositing account managing the archive on Zenodo.Statistical Impact: The blanket account deletion vaporized 862 scientific works and instantly broke 1,817 Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) across versioned records and ancillary data.Attribution Severance: A subsequent DataCite API investigation on June 20, 2026, revealed that 941 of those DOIs were made entirely invisible to standard creator-name searches. The remaining 737 DOIs were cast into a findable but broken state, resolving only to HTTP 410 Gone tombstone pages. The author's identity and names were completely uncoupled from the persistent identifiers.4.
